headline: Nebraska sends medical cannabis fees to attorney general, unchanged
dek: Two years after voters approved medical cannabis, Nebraska's commission sent a fee plan to AG Mike Hilgers despite growers' pleas, as Sen. McKinney plans a 2027 legalization bill.
key_points: Nebraska's Medical Cannabis Commission sent proposed rules and fees to Attorney General Mike Hilgers this week without the cuts the state's four licensed growers asked for, MJBizDaily reported, citing the Omaha World-Herald.
The plan would charge $20,000 for a cultivator or manufacturer licence, $15,000 for a dispensary and $13,000 more for seed-to-sale tracking, with renewals of $18,000 to $28,500.
No testing labs or dispensaries are licensed yet, so the four growers have nowhere to sell; the commission will not license more businesses until fees are approved.
Separately, Sen. Terrell McKinney of Omaha told The Marijuana Herald he will file an adult-use legalization bill for the session that starts on 6 January 2027.
body: Nebraska's medical cannabis market moved one step closer to having a price list this week, but not to having a launch date. The state Medical Cannabis Commission sent its proposed rules, including a full fee schedule, to Attorney General Mike Hilgers without making the changes requested by the state's four licensed cultivators, MJBizDaily reported on 18 November, citing the Omaha World-Herald. After the attorney general, the rules go to Gov. Jim Pillen for final approval.

The commission has said it will not license dispensaries, testing labs or other operators until the fee structure is approved. That leaves the four growers that began operating this year with plants in the ground and no legal buyer: there are no licensed labs to test their product and no stores to sell it.

Under the plan sent to Hilgers, according to MJBizDaily, the state would charge $20,000 for a cultivator or manufacturer licence, $15,000 for a dispensary, $10,000 for a transporter and $5,000 to join the production chain. Every licensee would also pay a separate $13,000 for seed-to-sale tracking. Renewal fees would run from $18,000 to $28,500.

By our arithmetic, a business holding a cultivator licence would owe $33,000 in its first year once the tracking fee is added, and a dispensary $28,000, before rent, staff or product. No fees have been collected yet, because the seed-to-sale system itself is still pending.

The growers asked for lower fees, or for payment to be deferred until they have revenue. In a joint letter last month, quoted by the World-Herald, they warned that fees out of line with any path to revenue could put existing businesses at risk and force the state to license replacement operators, delaying patients further. The commission did not change the plan.
> Nebraska has licensed growers before it licensed anyone who can test or sell what they grow.
## One of the strictest programmes in the country

The fee fight sits on top of rules that already limit the market. Cultivators may have no more than 1,250 flowering plants. Edible, vaporisable and smokeable products are banned, which suggests tinctures, patches and transdermal oils may be the only products on offer when sales begin, MJBizDaily said. The state caps dispensaries at 12, allotted by judicial district.

That allotment produces uneven access. The Nebraska Examiner calculated, as cited by MJBizDaily, that it means one dispensary for 584,526 residents in Douglas County, home to Omaha, against one for 112,979 residents in the district covering Buffalo and Hall counties. As we reported on 11 November, the testing side of the market is also still being built.

Voters approved medical cannabis in November 2024, with about 71% backing legalisation and 67% supporting a separate measure to set up the regulatory framework, The Marijuana Herald reported. Advocates accuse Pillen and Hilgers, who both opposed the campaign, of slowing the launch deliberately. For comparison, Kentucky legalised medical cannabis by a law signed in March 2023, opened the programme on 1 January 2025 and rang up first sales that December, MJBizDaily noted. Nebraska is now past two years with no sales date.

The slow medical rollout has not stopped talk of going further. Sen. Terrell McKinney, who represents Omaha's District 11 in the unicameral legislature, told The Marijuana Herald on 18 November that he will introduce an adult-use legalisation bill in 2027. He said the aim is to bring Nebraska in line with neighbouring states, raise new revenue and help people harmed by prohibition. He said he has had preliminary talks with colleagues and plans fuller discussions before the session.

McKinney has tried before. In the 2024 special session he filed LB 71, which would have created a regulated market with a 16% tax and a path to relief for some past convictions. In 2025 he filed LB 705, combining changes to the medical law with conviction clean-slate provisions; it was indefinitely postponed in April 2026. Nebraska's 2027 session begins on 6 January.

For the four licensed growers, every month without labs or stores is a month of costs with no revenue, and the fee plan adds to that bill. For patients, the product limits and the 12-store cap mean access will stay narrow even after launch. For investors, Nebraska remains a slow, low-volume medical market, and an adult-use bill from a minority-party senator faces long odds in a legislature that has resisted even the voter-approved programme. That last point is our assessment.

Watch for Hilgers' review and Pillen's sign-off on the fee rules, and for the first testing lab and dispensary licences that would follow. Watch whether the commission revisits fees under pressure from growers. And watch for McKinney's bill when the session opens on 6 January 2027.
